item.title: Bitcoiners - Live From Bitcoin Beach – How El Salvador Is Making Bitcoin Self-Custody Work Without a Bank, Data or a Smartphone! | Darvin Otero of Tiankii
item.description:
What does it take for 120 families in El Zonte to pay their social housing loans in Bitcoin, or for a hotel on Cloudbeds to take it at booking?

You’ve heard El Salvador put Bitcoin in front of a whole country. What’s harder to see from outside is which tools people are actually using now.

Mike sat down with Darvin Otero of Tiankii, one of the first local Bitcoin builders in El Salvador and a Bitcoiner since before the Bitcoin Law.

Darvin’s team started with tap-to-pay cards for people with no smartphone or no data, back when El Salvador became the Lightning Network’s first nationwide test. For the last year and a half they’ve focused on self custody, and Darvin explains how a self custody wallet on Spark can collect payments while it’s offline.

That work feeds the Bitcoin Payment Hub, a pre-printed QR code payment stand that stays dormant until a merchant connects a wallet. Each code carries a short Lightning address that works from a feature phone, and one feature exists because of the cracked phone cameras Darvin kept seeing at checkout.

Most hotels in El Zonte run on Cloudbeds, where paying in Bitcoin used to mean messaging the front desk and waiting for someone to send a QR code. Card fees in the region run 5 to 8%. Tiankii now puts Bitcoin inside the booking itself.

In the housing project, each family’s loan is in dollars and paid in Bitcoin, and their QR code doubles as their loan number. Some families don’t earn Bitcoin yet, so they can pay cash at a K1 ATM. Darvin also describes what happens when a parent working far from home wants to cover the payment...

He’s proud of the Salvadoran talent coming out of Cubo Plus and the Bitcoin Office, and of new circular economies in Chalatenango and Suchitoto. He’d still like more places to pay, and he’s watching grants go everywhere except to Salvadoran developers.

These are Salvadorans building the tools their own neighbors pay with, bear market or bull market!

If you run a hotel, a shop or a dev team, listen to this one before you decide what Bitcoin can do in El Salvador.


—Bitcoin Beach Team

From The Daily Wolf with Scott Melker, live weekdays at 12pm ET on Yahoo Finance.

Strategy, the world's largest corporate Bitcoin holder, is being dropped from MSCI's stock indexes under a rule that targets companies built mainly to hold an asset rather than run a business. Scott explains why that's not what sent Bitcoin down to $67,000 overnight. He also covers new bipartisan SEC and CFTC nominees, a rare moment of regulatory agreement, South Korea's new power to freeze crypto before a hack is confirmed, and a BlackRock-backed facility giving institutions weekend access to a tokenized fund.

Bitcoin Takeover Podcast – S17 E51: Martti Malmi on Iris, NostrVPN and Freedom Tech
item.description:
We recorded this at Bitcoin Amsterdam, the Bitcoin Magazine conference, with legendary cypherpunk and Satoshi contributor Martti Malmi. This is his second time on the show. Two years ago in Prague we talked about 2009, the forum, and the man who signed his emails Satoshi Nakamoto. This time I had promised we would talk about what he is building now. The conference still put him on a history panel.

Martti would rather talk about Iris, the Nostr client at iris.to, and especially NostrVPN, which he describes as Tailscale without the Tailscale company: your devices find each other on Nostr, with no email login and no coordination server. Underneath is FIPS, an ad-hoc mesh routing protocol. He also walks through Iris Chat, Iris Drive, git.iris.to, Hashtree, and a directory of about 20 apps at apps.iris.to. He is not making money from any of it, and he does not think software is a great business model anymore. Finnish people, he says, tend to be a bit ideological and not great businessmen. Maybe he is the same way.

We talk about Nostr in a bear market, about building for AI agents versus building for humans, and about permissionlessness as the reason an agent might pick Nostr at all. I put my usual heresy to him, that Bitcoin is now a family of projects, and he stays open-minded: if network effects dissolve, funds may gravitate to the best store of value and the best way to pay, and the biggest network may matter less. For him, Bitcoin is still mostly a store of value. He would like to tap to pay and not have to tell the merchant he wants to pay in Bitcoin.

We do break the "no Satoshi" rule twice. Martti is the one who set bitcoin.org up on WordPress, and he still thinks the man who struggled with that setup was "just a guy," unless you prefer the joke that the integer overflow bug was planted to make a time-travelling AI look human. And he remembers Satoshi paying him for the website work in US dollars, in an envelope, sent to his father's address so it would not sit on a dorm floor. He does not have the original envelope. His grandfather, in 2009, thought this could become a global reserve currency, and did not buy any. Years later, after another crash headline, his father messaged him: "I hope you sold early." And he did.

In between there is the year he stopped writing code himself, "meat agents" in smart glasses, a romantic argument that the best life extension technology is having kids, Michael Pollan on simulated feeling, and a fifty-percent kind of optimism about permissionless tech. You can find him on Nostr as Sirius, at iris.to/sirius. The name comes from the pun, the star, and Sirius Black.

What we cover:

  • Why history panels still haunt him, and why he wanted to shill the new work
  • NostrVPN as a peer-to-peer Tailscale alternative, and FIPS mesh routing
  • Iris Chat, Iris Drive, git.iris.to, Hashtree, and the apps.iris.to directory
  • Why he is not trying to make money from software
  • Nostr's chicken-and-egg problem, bots, and a bet on agentic use
  • Whether we are building for humans or for agents
  • Bitcoin as a family of projects, and dissolving network effects
  • Payments, Lightning, Square, BTCPay, and tap to pay
  • The bitcoin.org WordPress story, and "oh, he's just a guy"
  • The year he wrote no code, longevity, and consciousness
  • Satoshi, an envelope of dollars, and "I hope you sold early"
  • How to find him: Sirius, iris.to/sirius, and the three links to try first

item.description:

item.title: Bitcoin, Fiat & Rock'n'Roll – Inside BNY: Why the World's Largest Custodian Is Betting on Digital Money
item.description:
BNY's Nader Souri on stablecoins, OpenUSD, tokenized deposits and the infrastructure connecting traditional and digital finance

Accepting a stablecoin gives a company another way to get paid. Once the token reaches the wallet, the treasury team needs a way to put the proceeds to work. It can keep the token for another payment, redeem it for dollars or invest the proceeds under its cash policy. Each choice depends on what the company can hold and how quickly it can move the money again.

Nader Souri, head of digital and corporate banking at BNY, joins Jonas Gross and etonec’s Jonathan Knoll for the Digital Money Interview Series. Souri and Knoll worked together on Libra, when BNY explored how it might service the proposed reserve. They recall bringing legal and compliance teams into the work early. Souri explains how familiar tasks such as holding reserves and managing cash gave the bank a way to assess the proposal, and why he wanted regulators involved while the design was taking shape.

BNY’s work with Circle shows how those roles fit together today. Circle issues USDC. BNY is the primary reserve custodian and gives institutional clients a way to ask Circle to issue or redeem USDC through the bank’s platform. Souri explains why BNY wants to serve multiple issuers and why the same company might use a stablecoin to accept a payment and a tokenized deposit or money market fund to hold the proceeds.

The conversation covers the launch of Open USD and Qivalis’s plans for a euro stablecoin, as well as BNY’s expansion of digital asset custody to select EU institutions under MiCA. Souri expects collateral and liquidity movements to reach institutional scale early, with cross-border payments close behind. For corporate treasurers, he sees a more immediate hurdle. A wallet has to connect to the systems that already track cash and record transactions. That connection matters when a payment arrives outside banking hours and the company needs to move the proceeds to the account it uses to pay suppliers.

BNY's Nader Souri on stablecoins, OpenUSD, tokenized deposits and the infrastructure connecting traditional and digital finance

Accepting a stablecoin gives a company another way to get paid. Once the token reaches the wallet, the treasury team needs a way to put the proceeds to work. It can keep the token for another payment, redeem it for dollars or invest the proceeds under its cash policy. Each choice depends on what the company can hold and how quickly it can move the money again.

Nader Souri, head of digital and corporate banking at BNY, joins Jonas Gross and etonec’s Jonathan Knoll for the Digital Money Interview Series. Souri and Knoll worked together on Libra, when BNY explored how it might service the proposed reserve. They recall bringing legal and compliance teams into the work early. Souri explains how familiar tasks such as holding reserves and managing cash gave the bank a way to assess the proposal, and why he wanted regulators involved while the design was taking shape.

BNY’s work with Circle shows how those roles fit together today. Circle issues USDC. BNY is the primary reserve custodian and gives institutional clients a way to ask Circle to issue or redeem USDC through the bank’s platform. Souri explains why BNY wants to serve multiple issuers and why the same company might use a stablecoin to accept a payment and a tokenized deposit or money market fund to hold the proceeds.

The conversation covers the launch of Open USD and Qivalis’s plans for a euro stablecoin, as well as BNY’s expansion of digital asset custody to select EU institutions under MiCA. Souri expects collateral and liquidity movements to reach institutional scale early, with cross-border payments close behind. For corporate treasurers, he sees a more immediate hurdle. A wallet has to connect to the systems that already track cash and record transactions. item.title: On the Record by Bitcoin Policy UK – Response the FCA: how should the cryptoasset regulatory perimeter apply to Bitcoin?
item.description:
How should the UK’s new cryptoasset regulatory perimeter apply to Bitcoin?

In this AI-spoken episode, we present Bitcoin Policy UK’s response to the FCA’s consultation on its proposed Cryptoasset Perimeter Guidance.

BPUK welcomes the FCA’s recognition that developing software or participating in a decentralised network does not automatically amount to carrying on a regulated financial activity. But the response argues that parts of the proposed guidance need greater clarity to ensure that developers, miners, node operators and providers of non-custodial wallets are not inadvertently caught by rules intended for financial intermediaries.

The paper considers where responsibility should lie in decentralised systems, arguing that regulation should follow actual control rather than simply influence over software development. It also examines the position of Bitcoin and Lightning nodes, mining, non-custodial wallets and automated payment routing.

The response also looks at the treatment of Bitcoin payments, including payment processors and merchants accepting Bitcoin, and questions why Bitcoin payment services may face different regulatory treatment from those involving qualifying stablecoins.

The central argument is that Bitcoin businesses should be regulated for the financial services they provide, not simply for participating in or maintaining the Bitcoin network.

item.title: Quantum Bitcoin Countdown – Bitcoin Has Until 2032 | Isabel Foxen Duke QBC Ep. 13
item.description: BIP-360 proposes the first step toward a quantum-resistant Bitcoin: a new output type built to carry quantum-resistant signatures in a later upgrade. Which signature scheme follows, and how quickly developers can agree on it, is still under debate. So is Bitcoin ready for quantum, and how much time does it have? In the 13th episode of The Quantum Bitcoin Podcast, Bitcoin historian Pete Rizzo and co-host Nathan Jeffay put that question to Isabel Foxen Duke, head of the MARA Foundation, adviser to the Starknet Foundation and co-author of BIP-360, who says Bitcoin should be prepared by 2032 and that the push to get there has accelerated sharply in the past year.Episode 13 is the one that follows the fix through Bitcoin’s proposal process: how BIP-360 shrank from a single moonshot proposal into a step-by-step upgrade path, why some developers now question whether anything else deserves their time, and why she argues that for Bitcoin the conservative choice is to change the protocol. She explains the stateful and stateless halves of SHRINCS, the leading candidate for a quantum-resistant signature, why the safer stateless path could cost 10 to 20 times today’s fees, and why custodians and most wallets are expected to avoid the stateful path. It covers how miners are approaching the threat, why the first quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction calmed the market without settling the problem, what could happen to the millions of coins that never move, and the wallet habits that protect holders today. It closes with her response to Chamath Palihapitiya’s criticism of Bitcoin’s progress, her 2032 timeline, and why she expects shocks to the market even in the best-prepared case.The Quantum Bitcoin Podcast is a series examining the quantum threat to Bitcoin, designed to be watched in sequence. item.title: Bitcoin Well Podcast – BlackRock’s New Bitcoin ETF Is a Derivative of a Derivative | Adam O'Brien
item.description:
Bitcoin is holding above $80,000 heading into this conversation, 916 days past the halving, and the spot ETFs just bled more than $600 million in a single day without the price barely flinching. Q is joined by Bitcoin Well CEO Adam O'Brien, back from Bitcoin for Financial Services in Denver, to explain why the bigger story is what Wall Street is building on top of bitcoin.

Q argues that BlackRock's newly filed PBIT, a buffer ETF that trades options against IBIT to absorb roughly the first 10% of losses while capping your upside, is the mortgage-backed security of bitcoin: a derivative of a derivative, and the kind of product that could drive the next big crash. Adam walks through why Larry Fink came out of 2008 more powerful than he went in, what JPMorgan's first-ever bitcoin forecast (10% a year in the bear case, roughly 17% in the bull case) really tells you about bank incentives, and why a lowball forecast might one day carry legal risk. We get into Jamie Dimon's pivot from threatening to fire bitcoin buyers to pricing bitcoin into his long-term outlook, why ETF outflows aren't moving the price the way the headlines claim, and why every asset except bitcoin sits on the first rung of the counterparty ladder, including the option to hold real bitcoin in your IRA instead of the ETF.

This is a sharp conversation about Wall Street, ETFs, and counterparty risk, for anyone trying to understand who actually stands between them and their money.

item.title: #NotAnotherBitcoinPodcast – #NotAnotherBitcoinPodcast: Bitcoin Cash Fork Day — The Live Countdown (Aug 1, 2017)
item.description: How goes it? Five straight hours live on the day Bitcoin Cash forked off Bitcoin — and Kenn is on air for all of it, with the Coindance countdown on screen and under two hours to go when the stream starts.This is a working session, not a recap. Kenn tries to get at his BCC on his Ledger live (the Ledger Blue suddenly offering four different Bitcoin chains to pick from is a moment in itself), walks the chat through exactly how to sweep a paper wallet and split BTC from BCC with the Jaxx tool, and puts BTC's price on the record while he works: $2,775 on Coinbase.He also calls out the fork scams in real time — including a paid Facebook ad telling people to send their Bitcoin to a stranger's address to "receive" their forked coins — and says the thing that still matters: don't trust somebody else with your private keys. Personal responsibility era. Oh, and somewhere in there he agrees to give away 0.1 BCC, because of course he does. One thing he won't do: open his wallet on camera. Not happening.Super chats, the regulars in the chat box, and a front-row seat to the biggest chain split crypto had ever seen, caught as it happened — not remembered, not rewritten. Live.How goes it? Have a day.

Themen in dieser Folge:

  • Warum der Ausbau von Wind- und Solarenergie ein Netzstabilitätsproblem mit sich bringt

  • Drei Unternehmen, die das bereits umsetzen: Terahash, 21energy und Power2Bit


Die Anfangs erwähnte Studie der Cambridge University

item.title: The Café Bitcoin Podcast – The Finale: Liquid's 4,000 Bitcoin, the Caching Bug, and 50 Days for Freedom Wrapped
item.description:
• The last day. Brady opened with the count, 37 shows in 50 days, and the campaign's frame: political independence 250 years ago, monetary independence now. Yan Pritzker, Frank Corva, Suze and Alec on stage; Unseen Finance returned at the end.
  • The Liquid hack, plainly. On Sunday somebody sent 4,000 L-BTC to SideSwap's peg-out and the Liquid Federation paid out real Bitcoin. The L-BTC had been created from nothing. Blockstream paused the sidechain and 3,400 Bitcoin came back Monday.
  • ⭐ Yan on what broke: a caching bug, not anyone's keys. "The only two hard problems in computer science are naming and cache invalidation." Two transactions shared one cache key, so validators mistook a fake for one already checked.
  • Why it is not Bitcoin. Yan: Liquid is an 11-of-15 federation of companies with its own database and rules. "This is a separate thing, this is not Bitcoin itself." Lightning is built on Bitcoin script; Liquid is not.
  • ⭐ Frank on the 15%. The hackers returned 85% and kept about 600 Bitcoin. His question: will anyone be made whole, and if they keep it, "they're surely not white hats." A Bitcoin Policy Institute lawyer offered to talk.
  • Yan's verdict on the hat color: gray. Taking everything to beat a black hat is arguable. Keeping a cut is not. "You don't just return a wallet and take a bunch of stuff out of it."
  • Suze's question: Bitcoiners are ruthless about added trust assumptions, so why did Liquid get a pass? "Were we discerning enough?" Leave the base layer and you take on another code base and another set of failure points.
  • ⭐ Yan on open source in the AI era: it stays because every open project gets red-teamed by the whole internet. Closed systems get hacked too, "we just don't hear about them." The base chain is "the ultimate boss" nobody has beaten.
  • Yan's bank numbers, read live from the Identity Theft Resource Center: 3,332 reported data compromises in 2025 affecting 280 million people, 739 of them in financial services. "Bank-grade security" is not a standard anyone actually meets.
  • ⭐ Frank's hard question: must the layers be as bulletproof as Bitcoin? Yan: nothing is, and the only path is slow growth. Bitcoin was attacked at $1, then $10,000, then a billion. Early adopters carry the risk.
  • Yan's rocket-ship rule. Bitcoin Core engineering is closer to launching a spacecraft than shipping web software. "Years of careful review, study, simulations on other chains." Test new tech on other coins for two years first.
  • Suze asked whether ossification risks losing the skills to change Bitcoin in 50 years. Frank and Yan: no. Ossification is no new features, not no developers, and AI has widened who can work on cryptography and game theory.
  • Yan on open-weight versus hosted AI: the same debate as open source versus closed, and open source won the internet. His advice to companies: externalize memory, skills and harness so you can swap models. Swan built its own.
  • Unseen Finance returned with a proposal: these incidents are a credibility problem for the services on top of Bitcoin, not for Bitcoin. His fix, borrowed from banking: a self-regulatory body plus an insurance pool that service providers pay into.
  • Brady's tally at the close: Cory, Yan, Steve, Alec, Isaiah, Matt and Brandon from Swan; Larry Lepard three times; Parker Lewis, Daniel Batten, Tom and Callum, Guy Swann, Ryan MacLeod, Alana, Bob Burnett, Roxana. Suze made 35 of 37.
  • The close. "We have the tools, we have the knowledge, we have the culture, we have the determination." The half-price buy fee ends today; limit orders placed today keep it. Yan's last word: take security seriously, "go play with AI."

item.title: Swan Signal Live - A Bitcoin Show – John Haar Returns: Why the Fed Must Talk Tough While It Inflates
item.description:
• John reads Warsh's Jackson Hole speech as a nothing burger for Bitcoiners: a Fed chair must talk tough on inflation because signaling anything else would send inflation expectations and yields higher, while the long-run path of financial repression stays the same
  • Warsh reported that 54% of PCE basket components rose more than 3% over the past year, called 4.1% unemployment full employment, and framed inflation as squarely the Fed's problem to solve
  • Markets read the speech as hawkish anyway: the two-year yield rose about 12 basis points while gold and Bitcoin each gave back roughly 3.5%
  • On last week's expanded Treasury buybacks, John points to two signals: a 30-year yield near 5.3% is clearly bothering policymakers, and the Fed has never meaningfully reduced its holdings of 10-year-plus Treasuries even during quantitative tightening, evidence that natural buyers of long-dated government paper are scarce
  • The hosts revisit the shallowest bear market thesis they developed together on this show: a roughly 52% drawdown against 77% to 90%-plus in prior cycles, with the June low of $58,000 sitting just below the 200-week moving average before price rocketed back through it
  • John explains why he believes the June low will hold, while framing the 50-week moving average near $82,000 as the level the market is watching to declare a new bull market
  • Glassnode data shows 1.05 million Bitcoin of long-term holder supply with a cost basis between $83,000 and $86,000, the first heavy resistance shelf above spot, and the hosts discuss how cost basis shapes market psychology
  • The debasement trade is back in ETF volumes, with GLD and IBIT both in the top ten most traded funds, and the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio breaking its year-long downtrend after gold's 2025 outperformance
  • Bitcoin's long correlation with software stocks broke down in June, and John argues it was always the wrong frame, a point Lyn Alden's Wall Street Journal essay makes at length: Bitcoin is a protocol of value, not another technology stock
  • A broad Treasury ETF has returned roughly negative 18% after inflation over fifteen years while the supply of government debt keeps expanding, the picture John says is quietly ending the era of Treasuries as the world's default store of value

item.title: Meet the Bitcoin Taco Plebs - Bitcoin Magazine – Building Access To Bitcoin For Everyone w/ SeedSigner
item.description:
To be frank, I didn’t expect this podcast to be so profound! 

When I invited SeedSigner on to talk about his project, I was hoping to discuss all the cool technical aspects, his ideas for the future and Bitcoin 2022. While we touched on all of these awesome things, what I found really compelling in our conversation was the guiding principles of the project SeedSigner highlighted. 

Having access to Bitcoin, an open monetary network that does not debase your wealth, is a human right. Many countries or jurisdictions may stifle the bitcoin industry, making it impossible for some people to acquire hardware wallets that are otherwise common in the world. This project is an example of open-source software and engineering coming together to provide ever increasing access to Bitcoin. 

SeedSigner highlighted the importance of providing access to custody solutions that prioritize the DIY, verifiable and transparent aspects of hardware and software. While he did say that the project could potentially some day have a second form that would increase scalability and minimize self assembly, there are no solid plans for this now, as their full attention remains on the DIY side of things. 

One thing that stuck out to me from the conversation was his highlighting of the importance of fungibility and privacy. The two go hand in hand — if certain UTXOs are being labeled as criminal, those UTXOs must be subject to scrutiny that would deem them so. We also discussed if he thought CoinJoin and other similar privacy implementations are the key to this.

Of course, I can’t help but ask our current guests about Bitcoin 2022 — especially considering SeedSigner will be speaking there! If you haven’t already, please check out his article on his experience at Bitcoin 2021. In it, he details how it was his first real Bitcoin gathering, introducing his project and more.

At Bitcoin 2022, SeedSigner expressed his desire to continue to discuss his project with other people, but also, to finally catch up on all the other projects and happenings in the industry that seem to be flying by. I can fully relate to this feeling. 

Make sure to check out the entire podcast and follow SeedSigner on Twitter for more updates on this project. And of course, I hope to see you all in Miami!
